#+TITLE: Panoptes Research: Optimizer Deep-Dive — Architecture + Algorithm Upgrades
#+DATE: 2026-08-12
#+RESEARCH_ANGLES: 6
#+STATUS: complete

* Executive Summary

The single highest-leverage finding of this run: **the current 0.9936 IoU baseline is measured against a deterministically-corrupted cost term.** Angle 02 verified at the dispatch's line numbers that the distance-map index formula (distance_map_metric.cu:27, `blockIdx.y + gridDim.x` instead of `blockIdx.y * gridDim.x`) mis-maps every block row, so the distance-map term of every DIRECT_DILATION oracle evaluation accumulates at the wrong pixels. That is the one live bug of the seven verified — the other six poison latent paths only. Fixing it and re-baselining (one single re-baseline after all behavior-neutral fixes land) is the prerequisite for every other decision in this run: variant switches, perf cuts, and gradient polish are all judged against a baseline that is not trustworthy until this lands. The gate (IoU ≥ 0.85) is far below the measured 0.9936, so the appearance arbiter stays, but measured IoU / per-px L1 / the 6.31 mm z gap are informational and expected to move.

The recommended course of action, in dependency order: (1) pin-first fixes per angle 02 (Tier-0 pins, then behavior-neutral fixes, then the distance-map index fix + one oracle re-baseline); (2) the measurement apparatus per angle 03 — the z-profile probe on the RunDirectStage injected-cost lambda (cheapest instrument that sees the z-weak axis) and the production-shaped multi-stage oracle through the plan-006 OptimizerRunDriver seam; (3) the ablation runner + ablation.json as the scoring surface; (4) the evidence-backed algorithm upgrade from angle 01 — **1-DTC-GL-gb** (GL two-step Pareto selection + globally-biased refinement control), scored by the harness before any production switch; (5) compute-perf cuts 0–4 per angle 05, gated on oracle green and bit-identical cost values; (6) the differentiable-polish stage per angle 06, GO-gated on the z-profile probe and an ablation arm. Architecture work (angle 04) is the enabler that flows through this path as additive cuts A–E rather than a separate project.

Two tensions the user should carry explicitly. First, **the variant switch cannot fix the z-axis**: angle 01's GL recommendation improves search efficiency in 6-D at n>4 budgets (≈60–72% fewer evaluations, high-evidence), but angle 06 shows the 6.31 mm z gap is a magnification observability limit in single-plane fluoro — no selection/partitioning scheme changes what is observable, and a depth channel does not fix it either; the real z remedies are biplane (already supported) or a known-geometry prior, and every z remedy is gated on angle 03's probe. Second, **perf cuts do not sacrifice determinism**: angle 05 verified every active cost-path reduction is an int atomicAdd (order-independent, value-deterministic), so async copies and iteration batching can preserve bit-identical results — the docs' "atomics aren't bit-reproducible" claim applies to the DRR float-atomic path, which is not in the DIRECT cost path; a pose→score diff harness makes the bit-identity claim checkable per cut.

The "12x fewer evals" polish thesis should be treated as a target to test, not a justification: angle 06's analysis puts the realistic win at ~1.5–3× in the leaf/refinement phase (trunk 20k dominates the budget), with the chamfer distance-map surrogate as the one smooth gradient signal that exists in the codebase. Everything else from the papers — DIRECT-GLh hidden constraints, 1-DTDV boundary sampling, analytic-AA occlusion gradients, DRR-photometric gradients, torch bridges — is conditional, deferred, or NO-GO per the evidence below, and each lands only through the harness.

* Key Findings

** Finding 1 — The baseline is contaminated by a live kernel bug; one re-baseline is the run's critical path
- Angle 02 verified all 7 cost-path bugs at the dispatch's line numbers. Only one is live in the oracle's cost (DIRECT_DILATION): the grid→pixel index formula at distance_map_metric.cu:27 uses `blockIdx.y + gridDim.x` where the correct formula is `blockIdx.y * gridDim.x`. For the 64×64 crop / 16×16-block case: crop rows 0–15 are never visited, rows 20–23 are visited twice; the metric is deterministic but wrong. The IoU 0.9936 / per-px L1 0.0207 / z gap 6.31 mm baseline therefore includes this corruption in every evaluation. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, Bug 5]
- The six other bugs are dead for the oracle: uninitialized min_dist (DD_NEW_POLE_CONSTRAINT.cpp:134, UB read — can be a signalling NaN), Y_dist ≡ X_dist no-op (117–120), sym_trap tibia x→z (sym_trap_function.cpp:106), always-Trunk stage guard (CostFunctionManager.cpp:46 — tautology, makes DIRECT_DILATION_T1's branch/leaf behavior unreachable), Mahfouz pointer-guard + int truncation (implant_mahfouz_metric.cu:324/446, :93/122), curvature stub returning 0 + per-stage allocation leak. A dead duplicate DistanceMapMetric call sits commented at DIRECT_DILATION.cpp:101–104. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, Bugs 1–4, 6–7]
- Pin-first recipes exist for every bug: Tier-0 pure-surface pins (extracted helpers, CPU references) where a pure surface exists, Tier-2 GPU-labeled pins where the pin must observe the cost itself. All pins are red or spec-documenting today — that is the R13 characterization pass, and it creates the pure surfaces the fixes plug into. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, "Fix order"]
- Execution consequence: fix all behavior-neutral bugs first (zero oracle impact), then the distance-map index fix, then a single oracle re-run and baseline.json re-baseline. Only one re-baseline happens. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, Phase 0–2]
- Cross-reference: angle 06 explicitly warns new polish kernels must NOT copy the buggy index formula; angle 03's Tier-0 metric references must encode the corrected formula as spec. All three angles converge on the same critical path. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "Feasibility verdicts"; angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, Tier-0 section]

** Finding 2 — Measurement-first is unanimous across all six angles: no algorithm delta before the apparatus
- The doctrine (plan 006: "no algorithm deltas before the measurement apparatus exists") is independently restated by every angle as its ordering rule: 01 "no variant touches production until the harness says so"; 03 is the apparatus spec itself; 04's cuts A–E are each pin-gated; 05 gates every perf cut on oracle green + bit-identity; 06 ships polish behind enable_polish_ and lands it only when the ablation arm wins at equal-or-lower cumulative budget. This is converged evidence, not a single source. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, 03-measurement-apparatus.org, 04-backend-architecture.org, 05-compute-perf.org, 06-differentiable-polish.org]
- The current oracle cannot see what needs measuring: 3 frames, trunk-only, flat budget 3000, backface OFF — NOT the production shape, leaf z-refinement never exercised by any test, and a SetCallOffset or dilation-scheduling regression passes today. The multi-stage oracle (20k→25k→30k→35k cumulative, per-stage dilation, tibia-after-femur, sym_trap) driven through the OptimizerRunDriver seam closes that gap, with a stage-bookkeeping gate (costCalls() must land on 20k/25k/30k/35k) that the flat oracle is blind to. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "multi-stage oracle"]
- The driver seam is ready and green: OptimizerRunLaunch (by-value payload incl. 3 CostFunctionManagers), the OptimizerRunDriver interface, CreateOptimizerManagerRunDriver wrapping OptimizerManager untouched, and the controller's by-value relays (optimizedFrameRelayed) plus the oracle observation channel (costCalls/stageText/progress — "the oracle seam, M12"). One concrete seam gap was found: the typed Directive enum lacks SymTrap (needed for the tibia-ambiguity pass); a small seam addition is required. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "multi-stage oracle"; local-recon.org]
- The ablation matrix must encode: 7 registered variants × budget shapes (production 20/25/30/35k, reduced CI shape, flat-3000 oracle shape) × dilation schedules (6/3/1 vs 6/4/1 — itself an ablation axis) × backface ON/OFF × frames {0,1,2}. Cost profile: flat-3000 is "a few minutes" → ~20–60 evals/s → full 35k production shape ~10–30 min/frame → full matrix is hours, hence manifest-driven subsets: reduced shape per-PR, full shape nightly. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "ablation runner", "CI integration"]

** Finding 3 — The literature's highest-evidence algorithm upgrade is 1-DTC-GL-gb, and the current config is the literature's worst local-refinement regime
- Current repo config: original-DIRECT selection, ε=0, selecting ALL hull ties, 1-DTC-alike trisection on the largest denormalized side, L2 size measure. Jones & Martins 2021: ε=0 "spends so many evaluations refining local minima"; the empirical study: tie-all selection increases "global drag". The repo sits exactly in the worst regime the literature documents for a 20k–35k budget. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 1; https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07150; https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.14912]
- GL (two-step Pareto) selection beats IO/IA by ~60–72% on n>4 problems; budget crossover: IO wins ≤500 evals, N-DTC-IO best ~1000–4000, GL best ≥4000 — the 6-DOF search at 20k trunk lives far above the crossover. Partitioning: 1-DBDP best n>4 average but needs diagonal-bisection rework; 1-DTC best GKLS median and minimal code change; 1-DTDV catastrophic for interior optima (141,999 evals vs 919 on Levy10) — a trap unless the pose optimum is confirmed near the range boundary. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 2; https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.14912 §4.1–4.2, Table 3]
- Refinement control (Mathematics 2022, 10, 3760): every restriction except -gb hurts 1-DTC-GL on 287 DIRECTGOLib problems; -gb is the only one that never hurt and is best on expensive objectives (GPU silhouette with dilation 6/4/1 renders is expensive). Restrictions hurt worst when f* ≈ 0 — the silhouette-cost shape. ε-style restrictions are doubly contraindicated (the ε|f_min| window collapses as f_min→0). Landing variant: **1-DTC-GL-gb**, ε=0, L2 size kept, bit-identical defaults preserved behind an Options struct. [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 4; https://epublications.vu.lt/object/elaba:143490244/143490244.pdf §3–§4]
- DIRECT-GLh (φ = f_min + d(x_min,x) surrogate for infeasible/NaN points) is near-zero cost — the distances are already computed by GL's two-step selection — and beats barrier/NAS methods 18/80 vs 29–53/80 failures on hidden-constraint problems. But the trigger is unverified: no finite-check exists anywhere in the C++ cost path, so whether the production GPU cost can emit NaN is unknown; angle 02's cost-path audit owns that check, and GLh is conditional on it. Today a NaN result poisons hull slope comparisons in ConvexHull (silent storage corruption). [Source: angles/01-direct-variants.org, Finding 3; https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02205 §2.3, §4.2.1]

** Finding 4 — The z-weak axis is an observability limit, not an algorithm problem; the probe is the arbiter, and the real remedies are biplane or a known-geometry prior
- The 6.31 mm z gap (vs 0.16/0.08 in-plane) is the run's load-bearing research problem, converged from prior runs. The mechanism: a z shift is pure magnification — at ~1.1 m source distance a ±15 mm shift changes scale by <1%, inside the 6 px dilation tolerance; the dilated-overlap family is nearly flat in z. [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "z-profile probe"; local-recon.org]
- The z-profile probe reuses the RunDirectStage injected-cost lambda (optimizer_manager.cpp:1225+): sweep Δz ∈ {−15,…,+15} mm at fixed truth for the other 5 axes, 31 cost calls per (variant, dilation, frame) — a couple of minutes total on the RTX 3090 — and report valley_depth = (max−cost(0))/(max−min). A z-blind metric shows a flat or off-center curve. This is the cheapest instrument that sees the z-weak axis, and it gates every z remedy (SAME_Z weight calibration, chamfer reweighting, leaf refinement). [Source: angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "z-profile probe"]
- Angle 06's verdict on the depth channel: the machinery is ~80% present (DRR fill already interpolates perspective-correct z; dev_z_line_values_ buffer exists), but a front-surface z/w buffer does NOT make z observable in single-plane fluoro — there is no target depth to compare against, the gap is the magnification limit (no gradient changes what is observable), and NVDiffrast intentionally does not backprop through z/w (issue #70). The depth machinery is worth it only as: occlusion-aware visibility gradients, a synthetic-depth loss in the harness's self-supervised arm, or the z-line-integral in the ML/DRR pathway. The real z fixes are biplane (calibration_.convert_Pose_A_to_Pose_B + biplane branch already exist) and the known-geometry prior (implant constrained to a registered bone) — matching the prior-run ML angle's finding 8. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "depth channel"; https://github.com/NVlabs/nvdiffrast/issues/70]
- This is the dispatch-requested contradiction flag: angle 01's variant recommendations (1-DTC-GL-gb) optimize search efficiency but cannot move the z gap — the two are different kinds of improvement, and the probe is the instrument that separates them. A variant-switch win on the harness must not be mistaken for a z fix.

** Finding 5 — The cost path is sync-bound (structurally confirmed, magnitude unmeasured); 3 of 5 D2H syncs are trivially async-able, and int-atomics make bit-identical results achievable
- Per monoplane eval: ~15 kernel launches (8 render + 4 fast-implant-dilation + 3 distance-map) + 5 synchronous D2H cudaMemcpy, all on the default stream, zero streams/events anywhere in src/. The 5 syncs classify as: 2 structural mid-eval (bounding box at render_engine.cu:781–785; fragment_fill at :786–790 — removable only via kernel-level change) and 3 terminal (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289–290; distance_map_metric.cu:110–114, :115–119) — async-able now, all targets already page-locked. Cost nuance: the pairs share drains, so the real exposure is ~3 host-block windows per eval. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "Sync-point inventory"]
- The existing ms/call meter (optimizer_manager.cpp:1272–1278) uses clock() = process CPU time: it excludes GPU time AND sync-wait time, so it systematically under-reads a sync-bound pipeline and cannot arbitrate the item-8 claim. Fixing the meter (Cut 4) is required before any cut can be demonstrated to the user via the UI. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "The ms/call meter"]
- Determinism: every active cost-path reduction is an int atomicAdd/atomicSub on single counters — integer addition is order-independent, so identical launch configs + inputs ⇒ bit-identical scores. This resolves the docs' "atomics aren't bit-reproducible" claim: it applies to the DRR float-atomic path, which is NOT in the DIRECT cost path. Consequence: async terminal copies and iteration batching can be verified bit-identical by diffing a recorded pose→score sequence; Cut 3 (fragment-fill removal) must preserve per-thread work for threads < fragment_fill exactly. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "Determinism"]
- The DIRECT loop is sequential but each iteration's evals are pairwise independent (TrisectPotentiallyOptimal evaluates 2×N centers from a pre-loop snapshot) — batchable with replay-ordered bookkeeping, no GPU kernel rewrite. Constraint: FastImplantDilationMetric writes INTO the rendered buffer, so evals must be double-buffered (second render output + duplicate score buffers); biplane gets a free overlap (secondary camera buffers are separate). [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "The DIRECT loop is sequential", "In-place metric composition"]
- nvtx: declared in pixi.toml, zero instrumentation, and -DLIBNVTOOLSEXT is dead config; the nvtx3 header-only API compiles with no CMake/link change (toolkit include path already on jtml_compute). nsight-compute is in the lock; nsight-systems is not (needs pixi add). Per-eval timing data from Cut 0 replaces angle 03's derived 20–60 evals/s estimate. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org, "nvtx", "Measurement protocol"]

** Finding 6 — The polish stage is feasible only on a smooth surrogate; GO for chamfer-gradient polish, NO-GO for photometric/torch routes; the "12x" thesis is likely overstated
- The production DIRECT_DILATION cost is piecewise-constant in pose (binary silhouette + int reductions): finite differences on it give zero/garbage Jacobians; there is no gradient to polish through it. The surrogate already exists: DistanceMapMetric is a mean-chamfer loss with a Lipschitz image-space gradient ∇D, and its analytic gradient is the standard silhouette gradient dL/dθ = Σ ∇D(p)·(dp/dθ), needing only the per-pixel triangle-ID + barycentrics FillTriangleKernel already computes and discards (~10 lines + one float4 buffer to stage them). Published relatives: arXiv:1906.07870, arXiv:2501.14918. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "piecewise-constant", "smooth surrogate"]
- Feasibility verdicts: silhouette-gradient polish on the chamfer surrogate — GO (MVP = forward differences, 6 renders/step ~1 week; then analytic Jacobian + ∇D kernel, 1 render/step, +1 week; reuses Render(), uploaded distance maps, injected-cost lambda; float accumulation; match production backface=true and leaf dilation 1). NDC z/w depth buffer — feasible machinery but NOT a z fix; only as occlusion/ablation enabler. Analytic AA / occlusion-aware gradients — research increment after the MVP shows a win. Photometric DRR-intensity gradient — NO-GO for now (+3–6 weeks, low expected value). Finite-difference on the production cost — NO-GO. Torch bridge — NO-GO on design merit (autograd buys nothing for a 6-DoF static-STL scatter-add backward; and torch is already linked into jtml_compute — the ATen include in CostFunctionManager.h is a smell flagged to angle 04). [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "Feasibility verdicts"]
- Hybrid loop: trunk 20k → 2×branch 5k → leaf 5k → RunPolishStage(current_optimum) → optional DIRECT re-seed around the polished pose (Gablonsky locally-biased DIRECT / DIRECT+DF-local-search literature). Plug-in point mirrors RunDirectStage, no OptimizerRunLaunch signature change (reuses the leaf CostFunctionManager), budget-accounted (every surrogate + verification eval increments cost_function_calls_ so DIRECT-only vs DIRECT+polish is apples-to-apples at equal cumulative budget). Deliberately NOT routed through the Stage enum — the always-Trunk guard bug makes it unreliable. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "hybrid loop"]
- The "~12x fewer evals" thesis: unverified and structurally suspect — the budget is trunk-dominated (20k of 35k), so a 12x total claim requires shrinking the trunk (the ML-initializer pathway's job), while a gradient method plausibly converges the leaf refinement (~10^2 steps on a smooth surrogate) several-fold faster. Realistic expectation to measure: ~1.5–3× on the leaf phase + tighter final accuracy + lower frame-to-frame variance, at equal cumulative budget, reported data-profile style. GO condition for production: ablation arm shows ≥ the IoU gate at equal-or-lower cumulative budget with no per-axis regression; precondition: the z-profile probe shows the chamfer surrogate's valley is deeper than the dilated-overlap valley. [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org, "12x thesis", "go/no-go"]

** Finding 7 — The backend seam evolution is additive-first and deliberately minimal: payload + StageScript + named derivations, no new layer
- The "backend" is already a stack of three seams (OptimizerRunDriver, Optimize()'s stage loop, DirectOptimizer's injected std::function). The target shape: OptimizerRunLaunch stays the single by-value payload, additively gaining the DIRECT Options struct; the stage sequence becomes a StageScript (vector of StageSpec: {kind, range, budget, repeat, cfm_index}) that the same Optimize() executor consumes; dilation/dark-silhouette derivation (DeriveStageCostParams) and the cost-adapter construction (BuildGpuCostAdapter) become named pure functions; DirectOptimizer's boundary stays std::function<double(const Point6D&)>. Explicitly NO RunBackend enum (the driver IS the run-level backend — the fake driver proves it), NO new CMake target, NO headless executor extraction until the multi-stage oracle demonstrates the driver seam insufficient, NO ML in the loop. [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "Target shape", "non-goals"]
- Dilation stays COST-owned: it is a derived property of the active CFM parameters (the "Dilation"/"dark_silhouette" name scan at optimizer_manager.cpp:237–345), not optimizer config — moving it would fork the single source of truth. The seam is the named pure function DeriveStageCostParams, called once in Initialize. This deliberately counters the dispatch's "dilation under optimizer configuration" framing. [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "Dilation stays COST-owned"]
- Payload evolution contract: additive fields are FREE (DirectOptimizer::Options defaulted = today's behavior; the fake-driver test records the whole launch by value and compiles unchanged); restructuring into nested sections is ONE gated signature-adaptation cut with the test updated in the same change; the driver interface, Initialize signature, by-value forwarding, the 8 binds, and the epoch/threadActive gate never change. Do NOT move the 3 CFMs to pointers (perf decision pending measurement; would change the fake-driver copy semantics). [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "Payload evolution contract"]
- The stage loop stays in Optimize() and becomes script-driven in place: the loop is the only algorithm policy among three interleaved work kinds (session/GPU state and signal emission stay in the manager). RunDirectStage stays the stage runner; its injected lambda becomes BuildGpuCostAdapter, with three consumers converging on it (production runner, z-profile probe, and oracle_test's hand-rolled twin at oracle_test.cpp:286–291). A future gradient-polish stage is one StageSpec + one new StageKind + its own runner branch — same seam, no StageRunner interface built today. R13 gap honestly recorded: Optimize()'s loop has no headless emission-order pin today (manager is GPU-bound); Cut B's evidence is parity + oracle green + jj diff relocation + the new pure-function pins. [Source: angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "script-driven loop", "R13 pin surface", "Migration sketch"]

* Contradictions and Open Questions

** Contradiction 1 — Dilation schedule: 6/3/1 (docs) vs 6/4/1 (code)
- Angle 02 resolved this with source evidence: the code implements 6/4/1 — settings_control.cpp:1201–1206 sets branch=4, leaf=1; settings_constants.h TRUNK_DILATION=6 / BRANCH_DILATION_DECREASE=2 / Z_SEARCH_DILATION=1 agree (consumed only by the experimental SettingsBridge); production OptimizerManager reads the per-manager "Dilation" runtime parameter. The 6/3/1 claim lives only in golden_oracle.org prose + baseline.json. Both agree on trunk 6 and leaf 1; the conflict is branch only (4 vs 3). Neither was ever runtime-captured (the flat-3000 oracle never exercises branch/leaf). Evidence favors 6/4/1 as implemented intent; docs are the stale artifact. Angle 03 treats the schedule as an ablation axis (data, not assumption); angle 04 requires DeriveStageCostParams to return exactly what the manager derives today. Resolution path: Tier-0 registry/constants pins → runtime probe → update golden_oracle.org + baseline.json to 6/4/1 or change settings_control.cpp:1204 to 3. [Source: angles/02-cost-path-foundation.org, "Dilation 6/4/1 vs 6/3/1"; angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org, "ablation runner"; angles/04-backend-architecture.org, "What Could Not Be Verified"]

** Contradiction 2 — Variant recommendations (angle 01) vs the z-axis (angles 03/06)

So with culling ON, each backface triangle paints exactly 1 pixel: (Lx, By) — the min corner of its projected bbox. Wait, size 1 means insideIndex = 0 → pxPixel = Lx, pyPixel = By. - Round 1 said: "BoundingBoxSizesKernel skips dev_backface[i]==true ... culling ON paints front AND back faces... culling ON can drop visible pixels". The ACTUAL mechanism: with culling ON, backface triangles contribute size 1 (one pixel at their bbox min corner) instead of their full area, and their projected coords still enter the image bbox. So the ON-vs-OFF difference is NOT "missing back faces" — the back faces are mostly NOT painted under ON (just 1 px each), whereas under OFF they are fully painted (point-in-triangle fill). For a closed manifold viewed from outside, the back-face triangle projections lie INSIDE the front-face silhouette, so under OFF they're painted over the same region (interior fill) — the silhouette BOUNDARY is nearly identical; the difference is interior fill coverage (OFF fills interior more completely where back faces project outside the front outline — only for concave/self-occluding regions). Also the bbox is identical ON vs OFF (both include all triangles). So the ON-vs-OFF IoU at the golden pose for a watertight convex-ish femur should be ≈1.0 with tiny differences at silhouette edges where backface fill contributes boundary pixels.

Hmm wait, one more subtlety: under OFF, dev_backface[i] = false for all → all triangles full-size. Under ON, backfaces are 1 px. So OFF paints MORE pixels. IoU(ON, OFF) = |A∩B|/|A∪B| — OFF ⊇ ON mostly, so IoU = |ON|/|OFF| roughly. If backfaces are interior, |ON| ≈ |OFF| → IoU ≈ 1. # JTML Qt5->Qt6 migration, hegel PBT, and oracle tooling recipes

Captured after migrating JTML Qt5 -> Qt6, adding a hegel property-based test
layer, and building the Tier-2 GPU appearance oracle (U6-U8). These are the
concrete, non-obvious steps that cost real time the first time.

## Qt5 -> Qt6 migration recipe

- **The conda-forge Qt6 metapackage is `qt6`, but pin `qt6-main` + `qt6-wayland`
  (`6.7.2`) in pixi**, NOT `qt = "6.*"` (the `qt` package only ships Qt5).
  `pixi add "qt6-main=6.*" "qt6-wayland=6.*"`.
- **VTK rebuild against Qt6** (`vtk_installer.sh`): switch `-DVTK_QT_VERSION=6`,
  `-DVTK_USE_QT6=ON`, `-DVTK_GROUP_ENABLE_Qt6=YES`, `-DQt6_DIR=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/Qt6`,
  and DELETE the stale Qt5 VTK `build`/`install` dirs before reconfigure.
- **CMake**: `find_package(Qt6)` + `Qt6::` (Core/Gui/Widgets, and `Qt6::Test` for
  QtTest seams); pixi configure/activation use `-DQt6_DIR` / `Qt6_DIR`.
- **API deltas that break the build**: `QRegExp` is gone from QtCore ->
  `QRegularExpression` (escaped `[\\r\\n]`); `QDesktopWidget`/`qdesktopwidget.h`
  are removed (drop the include, use `QGuiApplication::primaryScreen()` if needed);
  and **`QSurfaceFormat::setDefaultFormat(QVTKOpenGLNativeWidget::defaultFormat())`
  MUST run BEFORE `QApplication`** in main() (latent bug, louder on Qt6).
- **OpenCV stays on its qt5-linked conda build** while Qt6 is present: benign, the
  app links Qt6::Widgets and uses no OpenCV Gui. A qt6-linkage OpenCV would bump
  OpenCV to 5.0.0 (major API change), so deliberately avoided.
- **Gate the migration with the pre-migration oracle + headless suite**, then a
  bounded manual GUI smoke (event-loop-ran-without-crash on a real display).

## hegel property-based testing via CMake FetchContent (conda-forge GCC)

- hegel-cpp is a static lib pulled via `FetchContent` (`GIT_TAG v0.11.1`); it also
  downloads a prebuilt `libhegel_c.so` at configure time and needs a `uv`-launched
  Python `hegel-core` server at runtime (cached under `.hegel/`, auto-gitignored).
- **Two link-time fixes on the conda-forge GCC toolchain**: (a) link `dl`
  (`dladdr`/`dlsym`), and (b) **append** `-Wl,-rpath,${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/_deps/hegel-build/libhegel`
  because the conda toolchain does NOT honour CMake's `BUILD_RPATH` and the lib is
  emitted there at configure time. GNU ld accumulates `-rpath`, so the pixi lib
  path stays.
- hegel is runner-agnostic: call `hegel::test([](hegel::TestCase& tc){ ... })`
  INSIDE a Catch2 `TEST_CASE`. This is property-based testing (auto-generates +
  shrinks) — complementary to, not a replacement for, the deterministic Tier-1
  golden.
- **Deliberate deviation**: hegel is introduced via FetchContent, not pixi.toml
  (AGENTS.md convention). Documented as a swappable layer; gate it behind an
  option if offline configure must not break.

## Tier-2 GPU appearance oracle + label-origin convention

- The load-bearing gate is a **SILHOUETTE/IOU comparison**, not raw pose (DIRECT
  numeric convergence is noisy). Render the implant at the recovered pose and IoU
  vs a known-good label image.
- **Binary label TIFFs use a bottom-left y-origin** while the GPU renderer outputs
  top-left: `cv::flip(label, 0)`. Pin the frame<->label correspondence EMPIRICALLY
  (start-pose render IoU == 1.0), not by filename (names are often unaligned).
- Feed the oracle the **processed Frame outputs** (edge/dilation/intensity/
  distance-map), not the raw x-ray, or the search is misled.
- Oracle reads fixture-relative paths, so run it from the repo root: set
  `WORKING_DIRECTORY ${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}` or `TEST_WORKING_DIRECTORY` on the
  ctest entry (ctest defaults CWD to `.build`). Label `oracle` only, never headless.

## Conda-forge GCC overrides CMake BUILD_RPATH

A reusable cross-target gotcha: the conda GCC toolchain forces its own rpath as an
RPATH and ignores `set_target_properties(... BUILD_RPATH ...)`. Fix: append
`-Wl,-rpath,<dir>` via `target_link_options` on the specific target.

content.thinking:
Excellent. I now have precise line numbers: 324 and 446 (guards), 93 and 122 (2.55 truncation), 425 (host ×255.0), 450 (final weighting).

The render flow also confirms: `cudaGetLastError(); // Resets Errors (MAYBE DELETE TO SAVE TIME?)` at the start of Render() — so a sticky error from a previous launch IS cleared at the start of each render. So a swallowed kernel-launch failure in one eval's metric kernels would be cleared by the next eval's Render() call. But within a single eval: Render() resets errors → all kernels run → if a metric kernel launch fails (invalid config from degenerate crop), the error stays sticky until the next Render() (start of next eval) clears it. The cudaMemcpy calls at the end of the metric functions would return the sticky error (ignored), and the buffers hold stale values (from the reset kernels that DID run before the failed launch — actually reset kernels run first; if the reset kernel launches fine and the main kernel fails, counters are 0). OK.

Also `fragment_overflow_` — a pose with too many fragments → render fails → cost still reads whatever the buffers hold. That's another failure mode: fragment overflow returns cudaErrorMemoryAllocation but the cost function proceeds (RenderPrimaryCamera's return is ignored in costFunctionDIRECT_DILATION — `gpu_principal_model_->RenderPrimaryCamera(...)` no error check).

Now, the bounding-box D2H sync: `cudaMemcpy(renderer_output_->GetBoundingBox(), dev_bounding_box_, 4*sizeof(int), D2H)` — line ~781-785 per angle 05. Note the bbox is Read ONCE per render into host; the metrics use the host-side bbox.

Also: the bbox D2H happens BEFORE the fill kernel (StridePrefixKernel + FillTriangleKernel). So the metrics' crop math uses the bbox computed from triangle projections (including backface triangles — bbox atomicMin/Max run on all triangles regardless of backface). So ON-vs-OFF: the bbox is identical either way! The crop dims are identical; only the painted pixels differ. Good for the ON-vs-OFF IoU protocol: same crop, same grid — differences purely from painted pixel sets.

One more important check for the NaN audit: what does the bbox look like when the model is fully BEHIND the camera (tZ < 0 for all vertices)? The projection sX = (tX/tZ)*fx + cx — with negative tZ, the sign flips: a vertex at tZ=-1000 projects to +sX (mirrored). So behind-camera vertices STILL project into the image plane (mirrored) — the renderer has NO near-plane clipping and NO z-test (angle 05 noted "no z-buffer"). text:
Paris Flood    Lindsey Palm-Vlasak    Will Burton    Paul Rullkoetter    Scott Banks Thanks: This work is generously supported by the McJunkin Family Charitable Foundation Thanks: A. Jensen, L. Palm-Vlasak, and S. Banks are from the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at the University of Florida Thanks: P. Flood is from the Department of Computer Science at the University of Cambridge Thanks: W. Burton and P. Rullkoetter are from the School of Engineering and Computer Science at the University of Denver

###### Abstract

Dynamic radiographic measurement of 3D TKA kinematics has provided important information for implant design and surgical technique for over 30 years. However, current methods of measuring TKA kinematics are too cumbersome or time-consuming for practical clinical application. Even state-of-the-art techniques require human-supervised initialization or human supervision throughout the entire optimization process. Elimination of human supervision could potentially bring this technology into clinical practicality. Therefore, we propose a fully autonomous pipeline for quantifying TKA kinematics from single-plane imaging. First, a convolutional neural network segments the femoral and tibial implants from the image. Second, segmented images are compared to Normalized Fourier Descriptor shape libraries for initial pose estimates. Lastly, a Lipschitzian optimization routine minimizes the difference between the segmented image and the projected implant. This technique reliably reproduces human-supervised kinematics measurements from internal datasets and external validation studies, with RMS differences of less than 0.7mm and 4° for internal studies and 0.8mm and 1.7° for external validation studies. This performance indicates that it will soon be practical to perform these measurements in a clinical setting.

###### Index Terms: 

Machine Learning, Total Knee Arthroplasty, Kinematics, Normalized Fourier Descriptors

## I Introduction

Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA) is a standard procedure for alleviating symptoms related to osteoarthritis in the knee. In 2018, orthopaedic surgeons performed more than 715,000 TKA operations in the United States \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. This number is projected to increase to 3.48 million by 2030 \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] due to an aging population and increased obesity rates. While TKA largely relieves symptomatic osteoarthritis, roughly 20% of TKA patients express postoperative dissatisfaction, citing mechanical limitations, pain, and instability as the leading causes \[[3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\]. Standard methods of musculoskeletal diagnosis cannot quantify the dynamic state of the joint, either pre- or post-operatively; clinicians must rely on static imaging (radiography, MRI, CT) or qualitative mechanical tests to determine the condition of the affected joint, and these tests cannot easily be performed during weight-bearing or dynamic movement when most pain symptoms occur. Unfortunately, most of the tools used to quantify 3D dynamic motion are substantially affected by soft-tissue artifacts \[[6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8)\], are prohibitively time-consuming or expensive \[[9](#bib.bib9)\], or cannot be performed with equipment available at most hospitals.

Model-image registration is a process where a 3D model is aligned to match an object’s projection in an image \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. Researchers have performed model-image registration using single-plane fluoroscopic or flat-panel imaging since the 1990s. Early methods used pre-computed distance maps \[[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12)\], or shape libraries \[[13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)\] to match the projection of a 3D implant model to its projection in a radiographic image. With increasing computational capabilities, methods that iteratively compared implant projections to images were possible \[[16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)\]. Most model-image registration methods provide sufficient accuracy for clinical joint assessment applications, including natural and replaced knees \[[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21), [22](#bib.bib22)\], natural and replaced shoulders \[[23](#bib.bib23), [24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25), [26](#bib.bib26)\], and extremities \[[27](#bib.bib27), [28](#bib.bib28), [29](#bib.bib29)\]. One of the main benefits of this single-plane approach is that suitable images can be acquired with equipment found in most hospitals. The main impediment to implementing this approach into a standard clinical workflow is the time and expense of human operators to supervise the model-image registration process. These methods require either (1) an initial pose estimate \[[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)\], (2) a pre-segmented contour of the implant in the image \[[10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11)\], or (3) a human operator to assist the optimization routine out of local minima \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. Each of these requirements makes model-image registration methods impractical for clinical use. Even state-of-the-art model-image registration techniques \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] require human initialization or segmentation to perform adequately.

Machine learning algorithms automate the process of analytical model building, utilizing specific algorithms to fit a series of inputs to their respective outputs. Neural networks are a subset of machine learning algorithms that utilize artificial neurons inspired by the human brain’s connections \[[30](#bib.bib30)\]. These networks have shown a great deal of success in many computer vision tasks, such as segmentation \[[31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32), [33](#bib.bib33)\], pose estimation \[[34](#bib.bib34), [35](#bib.bib35)\], and classification \[[36](#bib.bib36), [37](#bib.bib37), [38](#bib.bib38)\]. These capabilities might remove the need for human supervision from TKA model-image registration. Therefore, we propose a three-stage data analysis pipeline (Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")) where a convolutional neural network (CNN) is used to segment, or identify, the pixels belonging to either a femoral or tibial component. Then, an initial pose estimate is generated comparing the segmented implant contour to a pre-computed shape library. Lastly, the initial pose estimate serves as the starting point for a Lipschitzian optimizer that aligns the contours of a 3D implant model to the contour of the CNN-segmented image.

![Refer to caption](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/fig1-flowchart.png)

Fig. 1: An overview of the pipeline for autonomous measurements of total knee arthroplasty kinematics. First, the data is processed through a convolutional neural network to locate the pixels belonging to the femoral and tibial implants \[[32](#bib.bib32)\], then, Normalized Fourier Descriptor shape libraries are used to determine and initial pose estimate \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], and lastly, DIRECT-JTA \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] is run on those segmented images using the NFD estimates as initializations for pose.

This paper seeks to answer the following three questions: (1) How well does a convolutional neural network segment the femoral and tibial implants from fluoroscopic and flat-panel images? (2) Can a Fourier descriptor-based pose estimation method produce useful initial guesses of 3D implant pose from the CNN-segmented images? (3) Can the Lipschitzian optimizer, given reasonable initial guesses, replicate human-supervised TKA kinematic measurements?

## II Methods

Data from seven previously reported TKA kinematics studies were used for this study \[[39](#bib.bib39), [40](#bib.bib40), [41](#bib.bib41), [42](#bib.bib42), [43](#bib.bib43), [44](#bib.bib44), [45](#bib.bib45)\]. These studies utilized single-plane fluoroscopy or flat-panel imaging to measure tibiofemoral implant kinematics during lunge, squat, kneel, and stair climbing movements from 8248 images in 71 patients with implants from 7 manufacturers, including 36 distinct implants. From each of these studies, the following information was collected: (1) deidentified radiographic images, (2) x-ray calibration files, (3) manufacturer-supplied tibial and femoral implant surface geometry files (STL format), and (4) human supervised kinematics for the tibial and femoral components in each of the images. CNNs were trained with images from six of the studies using a transfer-learning paradigm with an open-source network \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]. CNN performance was tested using two image collections: a standard test set including images from the six studies used for training and a wholly naïve test set using images from the seventh study, where the imaging equipment and implants were different from anything used in training (Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ II Methods ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")). We used both test image sets to compare human-supervised kinematics with autonomously measured kinematics. Separately, two independent groups utilized our software to assess the accuracy of TKA kinematics measurements compared to their previously reported reference standard systems using RSA \[[46](#bib.bib46)\] or motion capture \[[9](#bib.bib9)\].

![Refer to caption](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/fig2-dataset.png)

Fig. 2: Data from seven studies were used to train and test the TKA kinematics measurement pipeline. Color coding in the figure identifies how many images were used for the training, validation, and testing functions. Images from the seventh study were used exclusively for testing the measurement pipeline that was trained using images from the other six studies.

### II-A Image Segmentation

Images were resized and padded to 1024x1024 pixels. Images containing bilateral implants had the contralateral knee cropped from the image. Segmentation labels were created by taking the human-supervised kinematics for each implant and generating a flat-shaded ground-truth projection image (Fig. [3](#S2.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ II-A Image Segmentation ‣ II Methods ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")). Two neural networks \[[32](#bib.bib32)\] were trained to segment the tibial and femoral implants, respectively, from the x-ray images. Each network was trained using a random 6284/1572 (80/20) training/validation split. Augmentations were introduced in the training pipeline to improve the network’s generalization to new implants and implant types \[[47](#bib.bib47)\]. Each neural network was trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU for 30 epochs. The performance of the segmentation networks was measured using the Jaccard Index \[[48](#bib.bib48)\]. This calculates the intersection between the estimated and ground-truth pixels over the union of both sets of pixels. The ideal Jaccard index is 1.

![Refer to caption](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/fig3-seglabels.png)

Fig. 3: A representative fluoroscopic images is shown (a) with corresponding femoral (b) and tibial (c) ground-truth images created by flat-shaded projections of registered implant models.

### II-B Initial Pose Estimates

Initial pose estimates were generated from bounding contours of the CNN-segmented implant regions using Normalized Fourier Descriptor (NFD) shape libraries \[[13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)\]. Shape libraries were created by projecting 3D implant models using the corresponding x-ray calibration parameters with ±30° ranges for the out-of-plane rotations at 3° increments (Fig. [4](#S2.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ II-B Initial Pose Estimates ‣ II Methods ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")). Pose estimates were determined as previously described \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] NFD-derived femoral and tibial implant poses were transformed to anatomic joint angles and translations \[[49](#bib.bib49)\] and compared to the human-supervised kinematics for the same images using RMS differences for each joint pose parameter. The performance of this method was also assessed using flat-shaded projection images with perfect segmentation as a ground-truth reference standard.

![Refer to caption](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/fig4-shape-libraries.png)

Fig. 4: Femoral (left) and tibial (right) NFD shape libraries were generated to capture the variation in projection silhouette geometry with out-of-plane rotation \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. Initial pose estimates were generated by comparing the NFD contour from the x-ray image to the shape library.

### II-C Pose Refinement

A modified Dividing Rectangles (DIRECT) algorithm called DIRECT-JTA \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] generated the final pose estimates. This method of Lipschitzian optimization divides the search into three stages, the “trunk,” “branch,” and “leaf.” Each of the three stages was assigned distinct cost function parameters and search regions. The cost function used a computationally efficient L1-norm between the dilated contour from the segmentation label and the projected implant. Successively decreasing the dilation coefficient allowed the optimization routine to escape local minima, and the leaf branch served to find the optimal out-of-plane translation. Transversely symmetric tibial implants posed problems during registration because two distinct poses produced roughly identical projections \[[50](#bib.bib50)\]. Because of this pose ambiguity, the tibial implant was always optimized after the non-symmetric femoral implant. In addition to the dilation metric, the tibial mediolateral translation and varus/valgus rotations relative to the femur were penalized. Final implant poses were transformed into knee joint rotations and translations \[[49](#bib.bib49)\] and compared to the human-supervised kinematics for the same images using RMS differences for each joint pose parameter. Squared differences between data sets were compared using one-way MANOVA with post-hoc multiple pair-wise comparisons using the Games-Howell test (R v4.2.0 using R Studio, rstatix, and stats).

### II-D Pose Ambiguities and Registration Blunders

A blunder was defined as an image frame with the squared sum of rotation differences greater than 5° between autonomous and human-supervised measures. These blunder frames contain errors considerably larger than would be clinically acceptable and warrant further exploration. Blunders were analyzed with respect to the tibial implant’s apparent varus/valgus rotation relative to the viewing ray (Fig. [5](#S2.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ II-D Pose Ambiguities and Registration Blunders ‣ II Methods ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")). A probability density function and cumulative density function were calculated for the blunder likelihood. Due to the high likelihood of blunders in this region, an ambiguous zone was defined for all apparent tibial varus/valgus-rotation less than 3.6 degrees, which is the mean + 1std of the blunder distribution (Fig. [5](#S2.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ II-D Pose Ambiguities and Registration Blunders ‣ II Methods ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")). Squared measurement differences between images inside and outside the ambiguous zone were also compared using one-way MANOVA with post-hoc multiple pair-wise comparisons using the Games-Howell test.

![Refer to caption](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/fig5-histo.png)

Fig. 5: The histogram (left) shows the correctly registered frames (Hits, blue) and incorrectly registered frames (Blunders, orange) plotted as a function of the apparent tibial varus/valgus angle relative to the viewing raw. The probability plot (right) shows the distribution of blunders (solid orange) and the cumulative probability of blunders (dotted orange). The Ambiguous Zone is defined as apparent tibial varus/valgus rotations less than the mean + one standard deviation of the blunder probability distribution, capturing approximately 85 % of the blunders.

## III Results

CNN segmentation of standard test set images produced Jaccard indices of 0.936 for the femoral and 0.883 for the tibial components. CNN segmentation performance on the completely naïve test set was lower, 0.715 and 0.753, respectively.

The initial pose estimates were within the range of convergence for the DIRECT-JTA optimizer and offered a robust initialization for optimization (Table 1). The RMS differences for initial pose estimates on ground-truth images were smaller (better) than for CNN-segmented images, but the differences were mostly within a few millimeters or degrees. Due to poor sensitivity for measuring out-of-plane translation with monocular vision, the mediolateral translation had the largest RMS differences for both image types.

![\[Uncaptioned image\]](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/tab1-nfd-performance.png)

RMS differences between DIRECT-JTA optimized kinematics and human-supervised kinematics were sub-millimeters for all in-plane translations (Table II). Mediolateral translations and out-of-plane rotation differences were smaller when the pose of the tibia was outside the ambiguous zone. The RMS differences for the completely naïve test set were within 0.5 mm or 0.5 deg compared to the standard test set, indicating similar performance on the entirely novel dataset.

![\[Uncaptioned image\]](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/tab2-directjta-rms-diff.png)

There was one femoral blunder and 43 tibial blunders out of 392 test images. Using the definition of the ambiguous zone as apparent tibial varus/valgus rotation less than 3.6 deg, 11% of images have a tibial blunder within this zone, compared to 3.2% outside. Sixty-six percent of tibial blunders were due to symmetry ambiguities (Fig [6](#S3.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ III Results ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")).

![Refer to caption](/html/2205.00057/assets/figs/fig6-symtrap.png)

Fig. 6: The figure shows the same radiographic image with two registered tibial implant poses: (a) shows a correctly registered tibial implant, while (b) shows an implant caught in a local cost function minimum corresponding to a nearly symmetric pose.

One-hundred thirteen image pairs from an RSA study of TKA were used to independently assess the accuracy of the autonomous kinematics measurement for single-plane lateral TKA images. RMS errors were 0.8mm for AP translation, 0.5mm for SI translation, 2.6mm for ML translation, 1.0° for flexion-extension, 1.2° for abduction-adduction, and 1.7° for internal-external rotation. At a different institution, 45 single-plane radiographic images were acquired with an instrumented sawbones phantom that was independently tracked using motion capture. Comparing the motion capture and autonomously measured radiographic kinematics, the RMS errors were 0.72mm for AP translation, 0.31mm for SI translation, 1.82mm for ML translation, 0.56° for flexion-extension, 0.63° for abduction-adduction, and 0.84° for internal-external rotation.

## IV Discussion

Dynamic radiographic measurement of 3D TKA kinematics has provided important information for implant design and surgical technique for over 30 years. Many surgeons have expressed an interest in utilizing this type of measurement in their clinical practices; however, current methods are impractical. We developed a completely autonomous TKA kinematics measurement pipeline that can potentially provide a practical method for clinical implementation. This study sought to answer three questions, (1) How well does a neural network segment TKA implants from fluoroscopic and flat-panel images? (2) How well can an NFD shape library estimate the pose of a TKA implant given a CNN-segmented image? And (3) How well does a Lipschitzian optimization routine replicate human-supervised kinematics for TKA implants given an approximate initial guess?

CNN image segmentation of TKA implants worked well, with Jaccard indices greater than 0.88 for the standard test set, and greater than 0.71 for the naïve test set. Segmentation performance for the standard test set outperformed published examples by 0.05-0.1 Jaccard points \[[51](#bib.bib51), [52](#bib.bib52)\], with the naïve test set on par with other segmentation examples. The most notable decrease in segmentation performance occurred along the perimeter of the segmented pixel region, especially in areas where implant projections occluded each other. These imperfectly segmented perimeter regions likely affect the initial pose estimate and the DIRECT-JTA optimization solution since both methods rely heavily on the segmented implant boundary. Further improvements can be made for the perimeter segmentation results by introducing intelligent augmentations during training using generative models \[[53](#bib.bib53)\] and performing neural network bolstered contour improvement strategies \[[54](#bib.bib54)\].

Our initial pose estimates were satisfactory as an initialization for the DIRECT-JTA optimization, falling within the convergence region of ±30° \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. However, the performance for the ground-truth projections was not as good as the cited method \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], which achieved errors of less than 1mm for in-plane translation and 2° for rotation. The cited method utilized an additional refinement step for the NFD estimation, interpolating the apparent out-of-plane angles between nearest shapes in the library. This extra step was not done because only approximate initial pose estimates were needed. In addition, the current study incorporated a vastly larger set of implant shapes (36 vs. 2) and image quality and calibration variations. Distinct implant shapes manifest unique normalization maps, where there can be discontinuities or jumps in normalization angles which affect the best-fitting library entry (Fig. [4](#S2.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ II-B Initial Pose Estimates ‣ II Methods ‣ Joint Track Machine Learning: An Autonomous Method of Measuring TKA Kinematics from Single-Plane Images")) \[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)\]. These details are easily upgraded with additional code using previously reported methods but were not pursued because the initial pose results were well within the DIRECT-JTA convergence region. The initial pose estimates for the CNN-segmented images were not as good as for the ground-truth projections. This follows directly from the fact that the perimeter of the segmented implants was not as accurately rendered, leading to poorer results with the edge-based NFD method. Finally, the out-of-plane translation estimates were relatively poor for both ground-truth projects and CNN-segmented images. This translation estimate is extremely sensitive to model projection and edge detection details and can be adjusted for better results if required.

RMS differences between human-supervised and DIRECT-JTA optimized kinematics demonstrate the two methods provide similar results. In-plane translation differences of less than 0.8mm and out-of-plane less than 1.8 mm, indicate good consistency in determining the relative locations of TKA implants. Rotation differences of 4° or less for frames within the ambiguous zone, and less than 1.7° for frames outside the ambiguous zone, indicate joint rotation measures with sufficient resolution to be clinically useful. We observed two important characteristics in the measurement comparisons that will affect future implementations and use. First, we identified an ambiguous zone of apparent tibial rotations wherein there is a higher incidence of registration errors. These errors resulted in significant differences in measurement performance for the out-of-plane translations and rotations. This phenomenon, resulting from the nearly symmetric nature of most tibial implants \[[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13), [16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17)\] prompts either practical modification to imaging protocols to bias the tibial view outside the ambiguous zone or modifications of the model-image registration code to enforce smooth kinematic continuity across image frames and/or to impose joint penetration/separation penalties \[[55](#bib.bib55)\]. Second, we observed similar measurement performance for the standard and naïve test sets, which differed only in the superior/inferior joint translation. This suggests that the autonomous kinematic processing pipeline can provide reliable measures for implants and imaging systems that were not part of the training set, which will be important for application in novel clinical environments.

Two independent research teams utilized our software to evaluate the accuracy of our autonomous measurement pipeline compared to their reference standard methods using implants and image detectors that were not part of our training sets. In both cases, the accuracy results were comparable to results reported for contemporary human-supervised single-plane model-image registration methods for TKA kinematics \[[13](#bib.bib13), [17](#bib.bib17), [19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21)\]. Interestingly, the independent accuracy results appeared superior to our assessment of differences between autonomous and human-supervised measures of TKA kinematics. In both cases, the independent centers used high-resolution flat-panel detectors that provided better spatial resolution and grayscale contrast than most of the imaging systems included in our datasets. With images of similar quality, it is reasonable to expect similar measurement accuracy.

This work has several limitations. First, the image data sets resulted from previous studies in our labs, so there was no prospective design of which implant systems and image detectors should be included for a pipeline that generalizes well to other implants and detectors. Nevertheless, the naïve data set and the independent assessments, all involving implants and detectors not used for training, performed well and suggest that the method can usefully generalize to measurements of traditionally configured TKA implants. Future work is required to evaluate measurement performance with partial knee arthroplasty or revision implants. Second, many methodologic and configuration options and alternatives remain to be explored, and the current pipeline implementation should not be considered optimal. How best to disambiguate tibial poses and determine the most effective and robust optimization cost functions are areas of current effort.

We present an autonomous pipeline for measuring 3D TKA kinematics from single-plane radiographic images. Measurement reproducibility and accuracy are comparable to contemporary human-supervised methods. We believe capabilities like this will soon make it practical to perform dynamic TKA kinematic analysis in a clinical workflow, where these measures can help surgeons objectively determine the best course of treatment for their patients.

## V Conflicts of Interest

None.
